Nicknamed 'Captain Comeback,' this Naval Academy grad won the 1963 Heisman Trophy, served a tour in Vietnam, then led the Dallas Cowboys to two Super Bowl titles — who is he?
Roger Staubach: American football player and Navy officer (born 1942)

As students in 1930s Paris, this Syrian and Michel Aflaq cooked up a doctrine blending nationalism and socialism, then co-founded the Ba'ath Party — and decades later he was assassinated in Paris. Who is it?
This 44-day conflict in 2020 ended in an Azerbaijani victory over Armenia and the breakaway state of Artsakh, with the defeat sparking anti-government protests in Yerevan — what was it?
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War: Conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan (2020)
The first Iranian ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize, this lawyer and former judge was honored in 2003 for her work on democracy and women's, children's and refugee rights — who is she?

Held every March in Austin, Texas, since 1987, this tech-film-music extravaganza also spun off an EDU conference and a London edition — what's this festival, often shortened to a three-letter abbreviation?
South by Southwest: American annual film and music festival.
He ruled an isolated pocket of Roman authority around Soissons long after the empire lost the region, until the Frankish king Clovis I defeated and killed him — who was this last Roman holdout?
Syagrius: 5th century Roman leader at Soissons.
Formed in 2015 as a reformation of a party once led by Jacques Chirac, this conservative party, inspired by Gaullism, saw its 2017 presidential candidate place third — which party?
This movement campaigns for women to have the same legal right as men to go bare-chested in public, and also supports mothers' right to breastfeed openly — which cause?
Topfreedom: Social movement to allow female toplessness.
The son of Ivan III and Sophia Paleologue, this Grand Prince of Moscow annexed Pskov and Ryazan and captured Smolensk from Lithuania during his reign from 1505 to 1533 — who was he?
Vasili III of Russia: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1505 to 1533.
As East Germany's chief decision-maker for two decades, this communist leader demanded the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 despite Soviet reluctance — who was he?
Walter Ulbricht: Leader of East Germany from 1950 to 1971.
The New York Times once called him the country's best-known lawyer; this civil rights attorney is most famous for defending the Chicago Seven — who is it?
Harold Alexander, 1st Earl Alexander of Tunis
William Kunstler: American attorney and civil rights activist (1919–1995)
A Russian lawyer-turned-politician who chaired the Duma's Family, Women and Children Affairs committee, she drew attention in 2012 for drafting controversial LGBT-related legislation — who is she?
Created in 1946 and headquartered in Paris, this government-owned utility operates 56 nuclear reactors across 18 sites and was the world's largest electricity producer in 2009 — which company?
Électricité de France: French multinational electric utility company.
Which one below was born first?
George Grove (born 1820) is the earliest of the four. Grove was trained as a civil engineer, and successful in that profession, but his love of music drew him into musical administration.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
Earth (formed ~4.54 billion years ago) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Frank Kameny is an astronomer. Franklin Edward Kameny (May 21, 1925 – October 11, 2011) was an American gay rights activist.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Eugene Wigner is a mathematician. Wigner and Hermann Weyl were responsible for introducing group theory into physics, particularly the theory of symmetry in physics.
What is the atomic number of Seaborgium?
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Sg and atomic number 106.
What is the atomic number of Bromine?
Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
In what year was Abraham Maslow born?
Abraham Maslow: Maslow was a psychology professor at Cornell University, Brooklyn College, Brandeis University, The New School for Social Research, and Columbia University.
In what year was Larry Page born?
Larry Page: Lawrence Edward Page (born March 26, 1973) is an American businessman and computer scientist who co-founded Google with Sergey Brin.
In what year was Alexey Pajitnov born?
Alexey Pajitnov: Alexey Leonidovich Pajitnov (born April 16, 1955) is a Russian and American computer engineer and video game designer.
In what year did Omar Khayyam die?
Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
In what year did James Clerk Maxwell die?
James Clerk Maxwell: Maxwell's equations for electromagnetism achieved the second great unification in physics, where the first one had been realised by Isaac Newton.
In what year was Sodium discovered?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Ammonium chloride: Pfizer. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
In which country is Embraer E-Jet E2 family based?
Embraer E-Jet E2 family: Brazil. The Embraer E-Jet E2 family is a series of four-abreast narrow-body regional jet airliners designed and produced by the Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer.
Who is credited with discovering Lynx?
Lynx (constellation): Johannes Hevelius. Lynx is a constellation named after the animal, usually observed in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Newton's law of universal gravitation?
Newton's law of universal gravitation: Robert Hooke. This is a general physical law derived from empirical observations by what Isaac Newton called inductive reasoning.
Who is credited with discovering Pulsar?
Pulsar: Jocelyn Bell Burnell. This produces a very precise interval between pulses that ranges from milliseconds to seconds for an individual pulsar.
Who is credited with discovering Coma Berenices?
Coma Berenices: Conon of Samos. Coma Berenices is an ancient asterism in the northern sky, which has been defined as one of the 88 modern constellations.

First coined as a term in 1852, this pattern of continued drinking despite its harms affected an estimated 283 million people worldwide as of 2016, according to the World Health Organization — name the condition?
Alcoholism is the continued drinking of alcohol despite the problems it causes.
A balloon-like bulge at a weakened patch of vessel wall, it can turn lethal in the brain's circle of Willis or the aorta if it bursts — what is this?
Aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.
This deciduous shrub genus in the rose family comes in black, red, and hybrid purple berry varieties, all bitter enough to usually be processed rather than eaten fresh — which genus?
Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
This large bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists mostly — 70 to 90 percent — of bone. What bird is it?
Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.

This general medical term describes blood escaping a damaged vessel, whether internally or through a puncture in the skin, with the loss of more than about 15 percent of total volume proving potentially fatal. What is it called?
Bleeding is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels.

Naturally green and yellow with scalloped black markings, this small, long-tailed seed-eating parrot native to Australia is bred worldwide in colors from blue to white — which bird, also called a budgie?
Budgerigar (--ree-; Melopsittacus undulatus), also known as the common parakeet, shell parakeet or budgie, is a small, long-tailed, seed-eating parrot native to Australia.

Which German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist discovered oxygen — though Priestley published first — and identified elements like molybdenum, tungsten, and chlorine before reportedly dying of mercury poisoning?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele (9 December 1742 - 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
A sweet-smelling, dense, colorless liquid with the formula CHCl3, this solvent doubled as an inhaled anesthetic from the 19th century into the early 20th. What is it?
Chloroform (often abbreviated as TCM), is an organochloride with the formula CHCl3 and a common solvent.

This icy small body from the outer Solar System develops a glowing atmosphere called a coma, and sometimes a tail, as it warms and releases gases when passing near the Sun — name this celestial object?
Comet is an icy, small Solar System body or interstellar object that warms and begins to release gases when passing close to the Sun, a process called outgassing.
This bird family, the sole one in its taxonomic order, includes roadrunners, koels, malkohas, and coucals across roughly 150 species. Name the family?
Cuckoo are birds in the family Cuculidae, the sole taxon in the order Cuculiformes.
Mother of Princess Alia, this royal later remarried a senior PLO official in 1970 after her short-lived marriage to Jordan's king ended — who is she?
Dina bint Abdul-Hamid (15 December 1929 - 21 August 2019) was a Hashemite princess and Queen of Jordan from 1955 until 1957 as the first wife of King Hussein.

Distinguished by permanently erect front fangs and a habit of rearing up while flaring a neck flap, which family of mostly venomous snakes ranges from an 18 cm white-lipped species to a nearly 6-metre giant?
Elapidae (commonly known as elapids, from Ancient) is a family of snakes characterized by their permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth.

Combining lab and field science with strong ties to ecology and evolutionary biology, this discipline earned three of its founders a shared 1973 Nobel Prize for their work on animal behavior — what field is it?
Ethology is a branch of zoology that studies the behaviour of non-human animals.
Discovered in 1999 at a Dubna lab, this synthetic superheavy element (symbol Fl, number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name was transliterated from Cyrillic — which element?
Flerovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fl and atomic number 114.
This field of study examines how a country's physical geography shapes its politics and its relations with other nations — what field is it?
Geopolitics (from Ancient Greek g 'earth, land' and politik 'politics') is the study of the effects of Earth's geography on politics and international relations.
Nicknamed the 'benevolent dictator for life' of the language he invented, this Dutch programmer relinquished that title in July 2018. Who is he?
Guido van Rossum (born 31 January 1956) is a Dutch programmer.
This genus of the mallow family includes several hundred species prized for their large, showy blooms, and is sometimes known by the alternate name rose mallow — name the genus?
Hibiscus is a genus of common flowering plants in the mallow family, Malvaceae.
This medical condition occurs when the body, or a region of it, is deprived of adequate oxygen at the tissue level — what is it called?

Hypoxia (medicine) is a condition in which the body or a region of the body is deprived of an adequate oxygen supply at the tissue level. Hypoxia may be classified as either generalized, affecting the whole body, or local, affecting a region of the body.

Once found as far north as Texas's Lower Rio Grande Valley but now extirpated from the US, this slender wild cat comes in gray and red color morphs, ranging from Mexico to Argentina — what animal is it?
Jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi); or is a wild cat native to the Americas.
A 1983 MacArthur Fellow in mathematics, this American's work on Hilbert's tenth problem proved crucial to its eventual solution — now known as the MRDP theorem. Who is she?

Julia Robinson (December 8, 1919 - July 30, 1985) was an American mathematician noted for her contributions to the fields of computability theory and computational complexity theory - most notably in decision problems.
Depicted as the goddess Minerva, this Italian physicist became the first woman with a science doctorate and the first salaried female university teacher. Who was she?
Laura Bassi (29 October 1711 - 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.
Prized as one of the most profitable seafood commodities in the coastal waters where it's caught, this clawed crustacean spends its life in crevices and burrows on the sea floor - which creature?
Lobster are malacostracan decapod crustaceans of the family Nephropidae or its synonym Homaridae.
Its bell-shaped flowers give way to yellow or orange berries, but this nightshade genus is better known by the folkloric root that inspired countless myths and superstitions — which genus?
Mandragora (genus) is a plant genus belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Its three main jobs are converting food into usable energy, building macromolecules like proteins and lipids, and excreting waste — the chemistry that keeps every living thing alive. What is it?
Metabolism (from) refers to the set of life-sustaining chemical reactions that occur within living organisms.
Also called Indian mulberry, this tropical fruit tree contains harmful anthraquinones, and its foul-smelling fruit is mostly eaten only as a famine food — which species is it?
Morinda citrifolia is a fruit-bearing tree in the coffee family, Rubiaceae.
First linked by a Michigan doctor to farm wives sickened by isolation, this Gilded Age diagnosis grouped together fatigue, headaches, and a depressed mood — what condition?
Neurasthenia (from Ancient Greek (neuron) 'nerve' and (asthens) 'weak') is a term that was first used as early as 1829 for a mechanical weakness of the nerves.
Concerned with the most fundamental concept of all — being — this branch of metaphysics distinguishes non-repeatable particulars from repeatable universals like 'green' — what is the field?
Ontology is the philosophical study of being.
Named after a 17th-century French mathematician and physicist, this SI unit of pressure is defined as one newton of force per square metre — name the unit?
Pascal (unit) (symbol: Pa) is the unit of pressure in the International System of Units (SI).
One of nine essential amino acids we must eat rather than make ourselves, it's found in mammals' milk and acts as a direct precursor to the neuromodulator phenethylamine — which molecule is it?
Phenylalanine (symbol Phe or F) is an -amino acid with the formula C9H11NO2.

This natural process transfers pollen from a flower's anther to its stigma, enabling fertilization and seed production, carried out by everything from bees and bats to wind and water — what process is it?
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther of a plant to the stigma of a plant, later enabling fertilisation and the production of seeds.
Found in more than 200 species of mushroom, this inactive compound is a prodrug your body quickly converts to psilocin, a near-cousin of serotonin — what is it?
Psilocybin (4-), is a naturally occurring tryptamine alkaloid and investigational drug found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, with hallucinogenic and serotonergic effects.
What fat-soluble alcohol form of vitamin A — found in fish, dairy, and meat — is essential for vision, skin maintenance, and immune function, and is used as a supplement to prevent xerophthalmia?
Retinol is a hydrolytic metabolite of retinyl esters belonging to the group of vitamin A1 as an alcohol form.

This zodiac constellation, whose Latin name means 'archer,' is traditionally depicted as a centaur drawing a bow, and its territory in the southern sky contains the center of the Milky Way galaxy. What constellation is this?
Sagittarius (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the Southern celestial hemisphere.
About 90% of the body's supply of this mood-regulating monoamine is actually made in the gut, where it helps drive intestinal movements — which neurotransmitter is it?
Serotonin (5-HT), is a monoamine neurotransmitter with a wide range of functions in both the central nervous system (CNS) and also peripheral tissues.
Known by such nicknames as 'sour dock' and 'spinach dock,' this tangy Eurasian herb thrives wild in grasslands and is often used as a leaf vegetable — which plant?
Sorrel (Rumex acetosa) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the family Polygonaceae.
Developed from an earlier design, this variable-sweep-wing Soviet fighter-bomber served from 1967 to 1990 and was exported in variants like the Su-22 — which aircraft is it?
Sukhoi Su-17 (NATO reporting name: Fitter) is a variable-sweep wing fighter-bomber developed for the Soviet military.
Also called bush crickets, this insect family in the suborder Ensifera includes over 8,000 mostly nocturnal, leaf-mimicking species — which family?
Tettigoniidae are commonly called katydids (especially in North America) or bush crickets.

A phenylpiperazine compound in the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class, this antidepressant treats depression, anxiety and insomnia but carries a rare risk of prolonged, painful erections — which drug?
Trazodone is an antidepressant medication used to treat major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and insomnia.
Mammals, birds, amphibians, fish, and reptiles all belong to this subphylum of animals, united by a backbone and a braincase — what is it?
Vertebrate are animals with a vertebral column and a cranium.
Though classified as a woodwind, this conical-bodied instrument is usually made of brass and uses a vibrating single reed to produce sound. What instrument is it?
Xoloitzcuintle (or Xoloitzquintle, Xoloitzcuintli, or Xolo) is one of several breeds of hairless dog.
Named for the skull-shaped marking on its thorax and first classified by Carl Linnaeus in 1758, this large moth was immortalized on the poster for 'The Silence of the Lambs' — which insect?
Acherontia atropos: Species of moth. It is most commonly identified by the vaguely skull-shaped pattern adorning the thorax, the characteristic from which its common and scientific names are derived.
Scientifically named Gadus chalcogrammus, this schooling member of the cod family gathers in massive numbers in the eastern Bering Sea — which fish?
Alaska pollock: Species of fish. The Alaska pollock also known as Pacific pollock or walleye pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod genus Gadus and family Gadidae.
Nicknamed 'whip-spiders' or 'tailless whip-scorpions,' these arachnids have no silk, no venom, and a name meaning 'blunt tail' — they grab with their pedipalps instead of biting — what order is this?
Amblypygi: Order of arachnids. The name "amblypygid" means "blunt tail", a reference to a lack of the flagellum that is otherwise seen in whip-scorpions.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.
Known commonly as palms, this family of over 2,600 flowering plant species includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms mostly found in the tropics — what's the family called?
Arecaceae: Palm family of flowering plants.

Despite its name being something of a misnomer, this herding dog breed was developed in California and takes its name from imported collies that arrived alongside sheep from Down Under — what breed is it?
Australian Shepherd: American breed of dog. The Australian Shepherd, also known as the Aussie, is a breed of herding dog from the United States.
Making up nearly 40% of all known insects with around 400,000 described species, this order is distinguished by front wings hardened into protective cases called elytra — what creatures are these?
Beetle: Order of insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae; species widely consumed include mealworms and rhinoceros beetle larvae.
This flowering vine's dried fruit is one of the most commonly traded spices in the world, its heat coming from a compound called piperine — what plant?
Black pepper: Ground fruit of the family Piperaceae.

Commonly known as mad cow disease, this fatal neurodegenerative illness in cattle is caused by a misfolded prion and can spread to humans as a variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What is this cattle disease called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy: Fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle. The United Kingdom was afflicted with an outbreak of BSE and vCJD in the 1980s and 1990s.
Jointly developed by Pakistan and China as a lightweight fourth-generation fighter meant to eventually succeed the F-16 in Pakistan's air force, this jet's Chinese designation is FC-1 — what is it?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Sino-Pakistani multirole fighter aircraft.
This medical emergency occurs when the heart suddenly stops beating effectively, cutting off blood flow to the brain and other organs within minutes — what is it called?
Cardiac arrest: Sudden or unexpected loss of heartbeat.
Latin for 'little brain,' this hindbrain structure fine-tunes motor coordination and timing without actually initiating movement — what is it?
Cerebellum: Structure at the rear of the vertebrate brain, beneath the cerebrum.
Every animal cell makes this waxy sterol — the liver most of all — and it doubles as the raw material for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. What is it?
Cholesterol: Sterol biosynthesized by all animal cells.
This scale insect that feeds on prickly pear cacti produces carminic acid, the basis of the red dye carmine used in lipstick and food coloring — what is it?
Cochineal: Species of insect producing the crimson dye carmine.
Known historically as blue vitriol, this bright blue crystalline compound with the formula CuSO4 forms an octahedral complex when dissolved in water — what compound?
Copper(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. It forms hydrates CuSO4·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 7.

Named from the Greek for "dark blue," this compound's signature group is a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen — and its soluble salts, like the potassium and sodium versions, are infamously deadly. What is it?
Cyanide: Any molecule with a cyano group (C≡N)
Working alongside longtime colleague Ken Thompson, this American computer scientist co-created the Unix operating system and the C programming language — who is he?
Dennis Ritchie: American computer scientist known for Unix (1941–2011)
Made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram, which thin, savoury South Indian flatbread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar?
Dosa (food): Thin batter bread originating from South India.
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Known as the weeping fig and the official tree of Bangkok, this flowering plant native to Asia and Australia is often used as a biomonitor in cities — which species?
Ficus benjamina: Species of fig. The species is also naturalized in the West Indies and in the states of Florida and Arizona in the United States.
Before becoming Ferrari's Formula One team principal in 2023, this Frenchman co-founded a junior-racing outfit that won back-to-back titles with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg — who is he?
Called 'a bridge between the natural and social sciences,' this discipline studies Earth's lands, features, inhabitants, and how they all came to be — what is it?
Geography: Study of Earth's spatial information.
This waterfowl family member is smaller than a swan but larger than a duck; its young are called goslings, and a flock on the ground is known as a gaggle — what bird is it?
Goose: Common name for a group of waterfowl.
This Arabic word for a 'report' refers to the Islamic oral tradition of anecdotes preserving the words and deeds of Muhammad, ranking second only to the Quran in authority — what is it?
Hadith: Collections of sayings and teachings of Muhammad.
Often contracted from undercooked shellfish or contaminated water, this foodborne viral liver disease causes symptoms like jaundice and fever that typically last around eight weeks — what is it?
Hepatitis A: Acute infectious disease of the liver.
This hormone, produced by cells surrounding a growing embryo, is what's detected in pregnancy tests and sometimes secreted by tumors, aiding cancer diagnosis — what is it?
Human chorionic gonadotropin: Hormone for the maternal recognition of pregnancy.
Typically starting to work within an hour, this NSAID relieves pain, fever, and inflammation but can worsen asthma and, in later pregnancy, is considered harmful — which drug?

Credited with the oldest known systematic classification of chemical substances, this alchemist's corpus also contains the earliest instructions for deriving ammonium chloride from organic matter — who is he?
Jabir ibn Hayyan: Islamic alchemist and polymath (died c. 806–816)
Building his first firearm at age 13 in his father's gun shop, this American designer earned 128 patents and pioneered the autoloading pistol — who is he?
In this eye disorder, the cornea gradually thins and bulges into a cone shape, causing blurry or double vision often linked to excessive eye rubbing as a risk factor — which condition?
Keratoconus: Medical condition involving the eye.
Also called the Mediterranean black widow, this venomous spider is common throughout the Mediterranean region and central Asia — what species is it?

Latrodectus tredecimguttatus: Species of spider. Latrodectus tredecimguttatus, also known as the Mediterranean black widow or the European black widow, is a species in the genus Latrodectus of the widow spiders.
This Australian speech and language therapist and amateur stage actor helped King George VI manage his stammer — who is he?
Lionel Logue: Australian speech and language therapist (1880–1953)
Able to breathe air thanks to lobed fins and a well-developed internal skeleton, these freshwater vertebrates are considered the closest living relatives of land animals — what are they?
With horn-shaped fins on its head and one of the highest brain-to-body ratios of any fish, this filter-feeding giant may even recognize itself in a mirror — which creature?
Sold under the brand name Mobic, this NSAID in the oxicam family blocks COX-2 more strongly than COX-1 and ranked 27th among the most prescribed US medications in 2023. What drug is it?
Which Hungarian-American psychologist coined the term 'flow' to describe a highly focused, creative mental state?
Named for its rough alignment with the Moon's cycle — the two words are even linguistic cognates — this calendar unit varies from 28 to 31 days in the Gregorian system — what is it?
Month: Unit of time, usually 28 to 31 days.
The only mammal that's essentially cold-blooded, this burrowing "sand puppy" of the Horn of Africa also lives in an insect-like colony with a single breeding queen — what creature is it?
This reddish-brown, poisonous gas (formula NO2) is a key step in making nitric acid for fertilizer — and your gas stove quietly produces it while you cook. What is it?
Sold under the brand name Prilosec, this proton-pump inhibitor treats acid reflux and peptic ulcers — what is it?
Omeprazole: Medication to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease and other conditions.
Located behind the stomach, this gland is 99 percent exocrine yet still secretes insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar — which organ?
Pancreas: Organ of the digestive system and endocrine system of vertebrates.

Famous for the giant throat pouch beneath its long beak, this large water bird's eight living species range from the tropics to temperate zones, with some even flying inland to Australia's Red Centre after heavy rains — what bird is this?
Pelican: Genus of large water birds with a throat pouch.
This toxic gas, which smells like freshly cut hay, was responsible for tens of thousands of deaths as a chemical weapon in World War I — what is it?
Named after the American diplomat who introduced it from Mexico, this red-and-green Christmas plant is not actually toxic to pets — which plant?
Also known as face blindness, this cognitive disorder leaves a person unable to recognize familiar faces — even their own — while other visual skills stay intact. What is it?
Prosopagnosia: Cognitive disorder of face perception. Prosopagnosia should not be confused with prosopometamorphopsia, a disorder characterized by altered perceptions of faces.
Some specimens of this native European tree, whose acorns dangle on long stalks, are believed to be over 1,000 years old — name the species?
Quercus robur: Species of flowering plant.

Almost exclusively affecting girls and emerging by 18 months of age, this genetic disorder — usually caused by a mutation in the MECP2 gene — brings language and coordination loss along with repetitive hand movements. What is it?
Rett syndrome: Genetic brain disorder. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a genetic disorder that typically becomes apparent after 6–18 months of age and almost exclusively in girls.

Also called 'German measles,' this vaccine-preventable viral infection is usually mild but can cause severe birth defects — including cataracts and deafness — if a mother catches it early in pregnancy. What disease is it?
Rubella: Human viral disease. Rubella, also known as German measles or three-day measles, is a vaccine-preventable infection caused by the rubella virus.
Named after the Latin word for a small shovel, this flat triangular bone connects the upper arm bone to the collarbone and forms the back of the shoulder girdle — what is it?
Scapula: Bone that connects the humerus and clavicle.
Built with a ribless cartilage skeleton, skin-covering dermal denticles and five to seven gill slits per side, these fish first appeared back in the Devonian — what are they?
A hygroscopic crystalline powder (formula NaNO2) and the most industrially important salt of its kind, this compound is most familiar to us cured into processed meats. What is it?
Sodium nitrite: Chemical compound. It is a white to slightly yellowish crystalline powder that is very soluble in water and is hygroscopic.
This Polish-American DuPont chemist invented a super-strong polymer fiber and became the fourth woman ever inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame — who was she?
Stephanie Kwolek: American chemist who invented Kevlar (1923–2014)

Allowing one neuron to send signals to a neighboring cell, this junction can be chemical or electrical, with coupled electrical types creating synchronized brain activity via gap junctions — what is it?
Synapse: Structure connecting neurons in the nervous system.
The primary male sex hormone, this androgen builds muscle and bone, spurs body hair, and is even linked to mood, courtship display and dominance in both sexes — what is it?
Testosterone: Primary male sex hormone. It is associated with increased aggression, sex drive, dominance, courtship display, and a wide range of behavioral characteristics.

First identified in 1846 and nicknamed 'Peter Elam's disease' in parts of South Asia, this skin condition causing patchy discoloration is caused by an overgrowth of Malassezia yeast — what is it called?
Tinea versicolor: Skin disease. Tinea versicolor (also pityriasis versicolor) is a condition characterized by a skin eruption on the trunk and proximal extremities.
Named after the Turkish word for turban, which it was thought to resemble, this spring-blooming bulb belongs to the lily family and includes about 75 species — which flower?
The primary flavor compound in the vanilla bean, this phenolic aldehyde is now more often made synthetically than extracted from the real pod — what is it?
Vanillin: Chemical compound. Vanillin is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.
Named after the German city where it originated, this all-purpose gun dog breed was officially recognized in 1891 — what breed is it?
Weimaraner: German breed of dog. The Weimaraner is a German breed of hunting dog of medium to large size, with history going back at least to the nineteenth century.
Following her husband's death, this Russian economist and activist vowed to carry on his opposition work and now chairs the Human Rights Foundation — who is she?
Yulia Navalnaya: Russian economist and political activist (born 1976)
Which of these is the longest?
Boeing C-17 Globemaster III has the greatest length of the four (53 m).
Which one below has the greatest length?
Argentinosaurus has the greatest length of the four (35 m).
